title: Search Insert Position
description:
# Search Insert Position

Given a sorted array of distinct integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the index of `target` if it is already present.

If `target` is not present, return the index where it should be inserted so that `nums` remains sorted in ascending order. The returned index can be `0` when the target belongs before every value, or `nums.length` when it belongs after every value.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.

## Example 1

**Input:** nums = [1,3,5,6], target = 5

**Output:** 2

## Example 2

**Input:** nums = [1,3,5,6], target = 2

**Output:** 1

## Example 3

**Input:** nums = [1,3,5,6], target = 7

**Output:** 4

## Constraints

* `1 <= nums.length <= 10000`
* `-10000 <= nums[i] <= 10000`
* `nums` is sorted in strictly increasing order.
* `-10000 <= target <= 10000`

tests.description: Target found at the last index
Negative target inserted inside a negative range
Negative target before the first value
Target after a mixed negative-positive range

solutions.name: Half-Open Lower Bound
solutions.description:
## Approach

Search the half-open interval `[left, right)` for the first index whose value is greater than or equal to `target`. If `nums[mid] >= target`, the insertion point is at `mid` or to its left, so move `right = mid`. Otherwise move `left = mid + 1`.

## Key Insight

The desired answer is exactly Java/C++ style `lower_bound`: the first position where `target` can appear without breaking sorted order. Half-open intervals make `nums.length` a natural possible answer.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Closed Interval with Answer Variable
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a closed interval and keep `answer` as the best insertion position seen so far. When `nums[mid] >= target`, update `answer = mid` and continue left. When `nums[mid] < target`, search to the right.

## Key Insight

`answer` starts at `nums.length`, which covers the case where every value is smaller than `target`. Every time a valid greater-or-equal index appears, it becomes a candidate and the search tries to find an earlier one.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Exact Search Returning Insertion Point
solutions.description:
## Approach

Run a standard closed-interval binary search. If `nums[mid] == target`, return `mid` immediately. If the loop ends without finding the target, `left` has advanced to the first index whose value is greater than `target`, which is the insertion position.

## Key Insight

Even a failed binary search leaves useful pointer state. At termination, all indices before `left` are smaller than `target`, while all remaining indices are greater.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Recursive Lower Bound
solutions.description:
## Approach

Recursively search the half-open interval `[left, right)` for the first value greater than or equal to `target`. The base case returns `left` when the interval is empty.

## Key Insight

This is the same lower-bound invariant as the iterative version, but written as divide-and-conquer. The recursion is useful for teaching why one half can be discarded without losing the insertion position.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n)
